How Bioswales Work

§1 · What happens to rain on this land right now

When rain falls on sloped ground, most of it does not soak in. It sheets downhill, gathers into rivulets, then into channels, and leaves the property within hours. Whatever it picks up along the way — soil, fertilizer, road salt, manure — leaves with it.

That water is not gone from the world. It is gone from here. It arrives in the nearest brook, then the nearest river, then the ocean, having spent almost no time in the ground beneath your feet.

Two costs follow from this, and they arrive in opposite seasons.

In spring and after storms, there is too much water at once. Runoff that moves fast erodes what it crosses. It cuts gullies, undermines banks, and delivers a flood pulse downstream in a few hours instead of a few days.

In late summer, there is too little. A stream between rainstorms is not fed by rain. It is fed by groundwater slowly seeping into the channel from the surrounding land — a flow called baseflow. Land that sheds its rain quickly has little stored to give back. The well runs low, the brook runs thin, and the pasture browns first.

Both problems have the same cause: the water moved too fast to be kept.

§2 · What a bioswale is

A bioswale is a shallow, planted trench dug along the contour of a slope — level from end to end, so water cannot run along it. Soil excavated from the trench is mounded on the downhill side to form a low berm.

That is the whole structure. No concrete, no pipe, no pump, no moving parts.

Water running downhill meets the trench and stops. Held there, it does the one thing runoff never does: it waits. And while it waits, it soaks downward through the soil.

The three words on this report describe the sequence:

Slow it. The trench interrupts downhill flow and drops the water's speed to zero. Speed is what causes erosion; removing it removes the damage.
